clue.text: Copies of Spare? They're heartlessly abandoned

indicators.note: abandoned behaviour is wild and unrestrained, so the letters are thrown into a new order
with its heart gone, the word They're keeps only its first and last letters

parts.note: outer letters of They're give TE

explanation.surface: A question about copies of Prince Harry's memoir Spare, imagined dumped without a second thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartlessly' strips They're to its first and last letters, TE; 'abandoned' then rearranges SPARE plus TE.
explanation.definitionFit: Repeats are reproductions or duplicates, as when a broadcaster shows a programme again.

clue.text: Separate publisher engaged by one of the family

indicators.note: to be engaged by something is to be held within it, so the publisher sits inside the relative

parts.note: an uncle is a family member
OUP is Oxford University Press, a publisher

explanation.surface: A publisher taken on by a relative, read as a family business deal.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncouple is to disconnect or detach, as with railway carriages, a verb sense of separate.

clue.text: Nancy's very old-fashioned royal interloper

parts.note: Nancy is a French city, so its word for very is the French tres
passe means out of date

explanation.surface: Someone called Nancy describes a royal intruder as terribly outdated.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy looks like a woman's name, but it is the city in north-east France, so 'very' is given in French.
explanation.definitionFit: A trespasser enters land without permission, an intruder where they do not belong.

clue.text: H and M in America are drones

indicators.note: the letter is placed within the country's abbreviation

parts.note: US is the United States

explanation.surface: The fashion chain H&M's American branches dismissed as dull and droning.
explanation.walkthrough: H stands alone, and the M sits inside US: the 'in America' attaches only to M.
explanation.definitionFit: To hum is to make a low continuous buzzing sound, just as a drone does.

clue.text: Clean round South of France town

indicators.note: turned round, the French word is read backwards

parts.note: sud is French for south
T is an abbreviation for town, as in football club names like Mansfield T

explanation.surface: A tidy-up around a town in the south of France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South of France' reads as a region, but it is the French word for south, sud, which 'round' turns back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: To dust is to wipe away particles from furniture, a kind of household cleaning.

clue.text: Alternative belief's mistake essentially — not happening

indicators.note: the happening part is no longer there, replaced by the other piece

parts.note: an opinion is a belief
in means fashionable, what is happening

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its central letter, here the middle of mistake

parts.note: middle letter of mistake is T

explanation.surface: A wrong belief as an alternative view, its error rooted in something never occurring.
explanation.walkthrough: Take IN out of OPINION and put T, the centre of mistake, in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: An option is a choice among possibilities, one alternative you could take.

clue.text: About to turn over swine — I'm not sure that could be literal

indicators.note: turning over flips the word end to end

parts.note: re means about, concerning
a rat is a contemptible person, as is a swine
um is a hesitant noise of uncertainty

explanation.surface: Someone hesitates whether a pig could be taken literally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'literal' is a printers' noun for a misprint, not the adjective it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: An erratum is an error in printing, and a literal is a typographical slip in typesetting jargon.

clue.text: Note Jose Carreras read out?

indicators.note: something read out is spoken, so it is the sound of the word that counts

parts.note: Jose Carreras is a famous Spanish tenor

explanation.surface: A musical note sung by the opera star, or a written note he reads aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech TENOR and TENNER sound alike. A tenner is a ten-pound note.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenner is British slang for a ten-pound banknote.

clue.text: Americans drinking crap beer regularly — they've no right to take over

definitions.text: they've no right to take over

indicators.note: one who drinks takes something in, so the beer letters go inside

parts.note: US twice, for two Americans

indicators.note: taking every other letter of the phrase

parts.note: alternate letters of crap beer give RPER

explanation.surface: Americans swilling bad beer, followed by a complaint about people grabbing power.
explanation.walkthrough: Americans is read as US plus US, two of them, and the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of crap beer, RPER, go between.
explanation.definitionFit: Usurpers seize a throne or position without legitimate claim to it.

clue.text: He's back in stir — missus finally moves to a new location

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: to stir is to rouse

indicators.note: going back means the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: He, with the 's standing for is as a link

indicators.note: finally points to the end of missus, the one letter it ends on

parts.note: last letter of missus is S

explanation.surface: A husband is in prison again, so his wife finally moves house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stir' is slang for prison, but here it is the verb rouse.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehouse someone is to give them accommodation somewhere else.

clue.text: Wait to move to a new country

indicators.note: moving the letters round puts them in another order

explanation.surface: Someone told to be patient before emigrating to another land.
explanation.definitionFit: Taiwan is an island nation in East Asia, formally the Republic of China.

clue.text: Turn to seemingly good American novel

parts.note: a U-turn, so U
pi is short for pious, sanctimoniously virtuous

explanation.surface: Turning to a good American novel for reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American novel' looks like the definition, but American is A; the book is Thomas More's 1516 work.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopia is the famous book by Thomas More describing an ideal island society.

clue.text: Sailor at university overcome by gas

indicators.note: in an across answer, being overcome by puts the other piece in front

parts.note: argon is a noble gas
at with U, for university, placed inside it, as a student is in a university

explanation.surface: A student sailor knocked out by fumes at college.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argonauts sailed with Jason on the Argo, so the word names a mythical seafarer.

clue.text: King's lost child in city abroad

indicators.note: losing something means it is removed from the word

parts.note: Charles is the king, with 's for has as a link

explanation.surface: A king's child gone missing in a foreign city.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking CH from CHARLES leaves a city in Provence, France.
explanation.definitionFit: Arles is a city in southern France, famous for Van Gogh.

clue.text: Turn party round? Ex-PM describing Labour leader as toast

parts.note: your go is your turn

indicators.note: turned round, the word is read backwards

parts.note: a do is a party

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so the ex-PM surrounds the letter

parts.note: Edward Heath was a former British Prime Minister

indicators.note: the leader is the first letter

parts.note: first letter of Labour is L

explanation.surface: A political party gathering where a former Conservative PM talks about Labour's leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn party round' tempts reversing everything, but 'round' only reverses the party; Edward Heath was Conservative PM 1970-74, describing meaning drawn around.
explanation.definitionFit: Good health is a drinking toast, wishing wellbeing as glasses are raised.

clue.text: Engineer wows leaders but they're not to be trusted

indicators.note: to engineer is to contrive or rig, so the letters are worked into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Engineers impress party leaders, yet the leaders are untrustworthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Weasel words are deliberately evasive or ambiguous phrases meant to mislead.

clue.text: Mark with date daringly showing leg but not breast

indicators.note: acting daringly is reckless and wild, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A first date where someone boldly shows a leg but keeps covered up.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about clothing, but the definition is poultry: the leg is dark meat, the breast white.
explanation.definitionFit: Dark meat is the darker flesh of chicken or turkey, from the legs and thighs.

clue.text: Hurt roughly tailless stork

parts.note: to mar is to damage or spoil

indicators.note: with its tail gone the word loses its last letter

parts.note: about means approximately

explanation.surface: A stork that lost its tail is roughly injured.
explanation.definitionFit: The marabou is a large African stork with a bald head.

clue.text: In crate? Wrong — in the bag

indicators.note: something wrong is out of order, so the letters are put right in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Something should be in a crate, but it is actually in the bag.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in the bag is assured or guaranteed, an idiom meaning sure to happen.

clue.text: Plants are fine around wet areas, gardener ultimately admitted

indicators.note: fine goes round the other letter

parts.note: OK means fine
an are is a metric unit of area, A

indicators.note: a piece admitted is let in, placed inside

parts.note: fens are marshy wetlands

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the closing letter of gardener is used

parts.note: last letter of gardener is R

explanation.surface: Plants growing well in marshy ground, with a gardener let in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are' is not the verb but the metric unit of area, abbreviated A.
explanation.definitionFit: Oak ferns are small woodland ferns, a group of plants.

clue.text: Following stranger for food

parts.note: odder means stranger

explanation.surface: Someone trailing a stranger in search of food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stranger' is the comparative adjective, not the noun it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: Fodder is feed for livestock, a type of food.

clue.text: Left with lots of women round big city neighbourhood

indicators.note: the women surround the other letter

parts.note: a harem is a group of wives or concubines

explanation.surface: A man left surrounded by many women in a city district.
explanation.definitionFit: Harlem is a district of Manhattan in New York.

clue.text: Set in middle of the forest

indicators.note: the central letter of the word

parts.note: middle letter of the is H
the Forest of Arden is the setting of As You Like It

explanation.surface: A scene placed in the heart of a forest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like a description of a setting, but it is the verb meaning to become firm.
explanation.definitionFit: To harden is to solidify, as concrete or jelly does when it sets.

clue.text: Ordered a number to go out and about

indicators.note: about signals turning the result back to front
the number goes outside, wrapping the single letter

parts.note: ten is a number

explanation.surface: An instruction for a group to go out and roam.
explanation.walkthrough: TEN wraps A to make TAEN, which 'about' then reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat means tidy and orderly, everything in its proper place.

clue.text: Head abroad taking hot-blooded type, naked, as partner

indicators.note: taking something in holds it inside

parts.note: tete is French for head

indicators.note: stripped of its outer letters, the word keeps only its middle

parts.note: a mammal is a warm-blooded animal

explanation.surface: Heading overseas with a passionate, unclothed companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naked' strips MAMMAL to AMMA, which goes inside the French head.
explanation.definitionFit: A teammate is a fellow member of a team, a partner in play.

clue.text: Box, maybe one from Hebridean island

indicators.note: one is taken from the island, removed

parts.note: Tiree is an island in the Inner Hebrides off Scotland
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A box that perhaps came from a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a container, but it is the evergreen shrub or tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Box is an evergreen shrub or small tree, an example of the category.

clue.text: Stand a chance covering one note over with another

indicators.note: turned over, the letters are read in the other direction
covering something means holding it within

parts.note: a lot is a chance, as in drawing lots
re is a note in sol-fa
te is another note in sol-fa

explanation.surface: A musical exercise: standing a chance by covering one note with another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a chance' is A plus LOT, and 'over' reverses that whole envelope before the second note follows; re and te are sol-fa syllables.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand something is to put up with or endure it.

clue.text: Grace shown by Martha and Liam getting together

indicators.note: the answer is on show inside the names, so everything around it falls away
the two names get together, closing up with the joining word between them gone

parts.note: the two names, run together once the and is dropped

explanation.surface: Elegance displayed by a couple, Martha and Liam, when they meet.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a hidden word with a twist: 'getting together' squeezes out the and so the names meet as MARTHALIAM, and 'shown by' points to the answer straddling the join.
explanation.definitionFit: Thalia is one of the three Graces of Greek mythology, goddesses of charm and beauty.
